newsitem.title: USA: Ralston, Cohen hold Pentagon meeting on adultery.
newsitem.headline: Ralston, Cohen hold Pentagon meeting on adultery.

text.p: Air Force Gen. Joseph Ralston met with Defence Secretary William Cohen on Monday amid expectations Ralston would withdraw from consideration for the top U.S. military job because of an adulterous affair he had.

Ralston, 53, did not comment as he left Cohen's Pentagon office after the brief, inconclusive meeting to discuss a major controversy over Cohen's consideration of the general to become chairman of the military Joint Chiefs of Staff.
"No decision," Cohen tersely told reporters later when asked if the matter had been settled.
"There was no decision at the meeting. General Ralston is still studying his options," a defence official told Reuters. He said he expected a "flight or fight" decision by the general soon.

Other defence officials said they expected Ralston, vice chairman of the joint chiefs and a decorated Vietnam War veteran, to withdraw from consideration after his admission last week that he had an adulterous affair while separated from his first wife 13 years ago.
"The handwriting is on the wall. I think he wanted to fight this thing but it's just gotten too big," one official said of the highly regarded Air Force general.

Army Gen. John Shalikashvili, whom Ralston was earlier favoured to succeed in the top military job, told reporters on Monday he would not consider delaying his Sept. 30 retirement to remain in the post for another two years.
Cohen and the White House set off a heated debate, saying when the controversy broke last week that Ralston remained high on Cohen's list of candidates to succeed Shalikashvili.

Members of Congress on Monday continued to question the fairness of the military's uneven application of strict rules against adultery, warning that the Senate might reject Ralston if he were to be nominated by President Bill Clinton to become the nation's new senior officer.

Cohen said last week that Ralston's previous affair should not eliminate him from consideration because it had not threatened "the good order and discipline" of the military. He spoke only weeks after the Air Force forced 26-year-old Lt. Kelly Flinn, its first woman bomber pilot, to resign without an honourable discharge to avoid a court-martial on charges of adultery, fraternisation, lying and failure to obey orders.

"If you're going to have a standard you cannot selectively enforce it," Democratic Representative Carolyn Maloney of New York said on CNN on Monday. "You cannot have one standard for a woman and another for a man, or one standard for a high-ranking member of the military and another for a lower-ranking member of the military."

A senior Pentagon official said Cohen, who departs on a week-long trip to Europe and the Middle East on Wednesday, was not expected to recommend his choice for a nominee to Clinton until after his return. The official, who asked not to be identified, said a number of senior officers were under consideration including the chiefs of the individual U.S. military services and heads of commands around the world.

The controversy broke after Cohen repeatedly in recent weeks stood behind strict military rules involving sexual harassment while the Army is embroiled in a scandal over rapes of female recruits by male drill sergeants.

Aside from crimes such as rape and other harassment, many members of Congress are charging that junior officers and enlisted personnel are treated more harshly than senior officers in cases involving adultery.

"Our cases were very much the same, but we were treated very differently," Flinn wrote in a guest essay in Newsweek magazine this week, referring to the Ralston case. "What matters in these cases is not what really happened but your rank, your gender and who do you know."
